questions.q: The editorial quotes the Quran’s image of a torrent whose foam is carried off while “whatever is of use to man remains behind.” What does it conclude?
options: Rivers should be controlled by dams
Not quite. The article says: A community must prove useful – a “giver” that stands on merit – to hold a respected place.
The strong always sweep away the weak
Not quite. The article says: A community must prove useful – a “giver” that stands on merit – to hold a respected place.
A community must prove useful – a “giver” that stands on merit – to hold a respected place
Yes. Favours achieve nothing.
Wealth, like foam, should be thrown away
Not quite. The article says: A community must prove useful – a “giver” that stands on merit – to hold a respected place.
questions.rationale: “According to the above verse of the Quran, Muslims must prove themselves a ‘giver’ community.”

questions.q: King Roger II of Sicily had defeated the Muslims in battle. Whom did he choose to prepare his atlas of the world, and what does this show?
options: A Greek sailor – maps belong to seafarers
Not quite. The article says: The Muslim scholar Al-Idrisi – learning kept its honour even after military defeat.
The Muslim scholar Al-Idrisi – learning kept its honour even after military defeat
Right. Excellence in knowledge is the lasting strength.
No one – the atlas was never made
Not quite. The article says: The Muslim scholar Al-Idrisi – learning kept its honour even after military defeat.
A Norman monk – conquerors trust only their own
Not quite. The article says: The Muslim scholar Al-Idrisi – learning kept its honour even after military defeat.
questions.rationale: “Though defeated on the field of battle, Muslims continued their intellectual and academic dominance, even in the court of their conqueror.”

questions.q: Everyone is born unique, yet many never achieve what they could. What price does the article say must be paid?
options: A large sum for training
Not quite. The article says: Undivided dedication to developing one’s particular talent, setting other things aside.
Undivided dedication to developing one’s particular talent, setting other things aside
Yes. “To do one task, you have to abandon all others.”
Years of waiting for luck
Not quite. The article says: Undivided dedication to developing one’s particular talent, setting other things aside.
The approval of one’s family
Not quite. The article says: Undivided dedication to developing one’s particular talent, setting other things aside.
questions.rationale: “The uniqueness of the individual can be brought into light only after paying the due price… you must work towards developing it with complete dedication and undivided attention.”

questions.q: What does the article mean by becoming a “big bird” thinker?
options: Travelling far from home
Not quite. The article says: Rising above troubles as large birds fly above a storm.
Looking down on other people
Not quite. The article says: Rising above troubles as large birds fly above a storm.
Eating and sleeping well
Not quite. The article says: Rising above troubles as large birds fly above a storm.
Rising above troubles as large birds fly above a storm
Well read. So that setbacks do not stop the journey.
questions.rationale: “When a storm strikes, big birds fly well above the reach of the storm, and thus save themselves.”

questions.q: Besides scholarship, what does the article name as the most important key to understanding the Quran?
options: A knowledge of many languages
Not quite. The article says: God-consciousness (taqwa), which leads one to ask God Himself for guidance.
Membership of a learned family
Not quite. The article says: God-consciousness (taqwa), which leads one to ask God Himself for guidance.
Reading it at great speed
Not quite. The article says: God-consciousness (taqwa), which leads one to ask God Himself for guidance.
God-consciousness (taqwa), which leads one to ask God Himself for guidance
Correct. “Be mindful of God; He teaches you.”
questions.rationale: “There is another way to understand the Quran, and which is undoubtedly the most important. And that is taqwa, or God-consciousness.”

questions.q: The article likens human life to a flowing river, with new generations replacing old. What wisdom does it see in this arrangement?
options: The past is best forgotten
Not quite. The article says: The young can learn from the experience of their elders and so travel better.
The old are no longer needed
Not quite. The article says: The young can learn from the experience of their elders and so travel better.
Each generation must begin from nothing
Not quite. The article says: The young can learn from the experience of their elders and so travel better.
The young can learn from the experience of their elders and so travel better
Yes. The wise elderly are a gift to the energetic young.
questions.rationale: “Its aim is that the coming generation should learn its lesson from the experiences of the previous generation.”

questions.q: A poor man asked the Prophet for money. What did the Prophet do?
options: Gave him enough to live on for a year
Not quite. The article says: Gave him a little to get started and told him to cut wood, sell it and earn his own living.
Asked others to employ him
Not quite. The article says: Gave him a little to get started and told him to cut wood, sell it and earn his own living.
Gave him a little to get started and told him to cut wood, sell it and earn his own living
Right. “The upper hand is better than the lower hand.”
Sent him away with nothing
Not quite. The article says: Gave him a little to get started and told him to cut wood, sell it and earn his own living.
questions.rationale: “Go to the forest, cut some wood and sell it to earn your livelihood…” Two months later the man said: “Now I have decided not ask for anything from anyone.”

questions.q: Instead of a “silver spoon,” with what does the article say a fortunate child is born?
options: A wooden spoon
Not quite. The article says: An “incentive spoon” – hardship that spurs him to work.
An “incentive spoon” – hardship that spurs him to work
Yes. Comfort kills motivation.
A golden spoon
Not quite. The article says: An “incentive spoon” – hardship that spurs him to work.
No spoon at all
Not quite. The article says: An “incentive spoon” – hardship that spurs him to work.
questions.rationale: “Fortunate is one who is born with an incentive spoon in his mouth. If you are born to a life of hardship, it will activate you.”

questions.q: Helen Hooven Santmyer worked on her novel for decades, even from a nursing home, and won recognition in her eighties. What does the article compare with her labour?
options: A ruler’s wish for fame
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s lifelong effort, sustained by faith in the reward of the Hereafter.
A merchant’s search for profit
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s lifelong effort, sustained by faith in the reward of the Hereafter.
The believer’s lifelong effort, sustained by faith in the reward of the Hereafter
Exactly. Strong belief lifts one above circumstances.
A student’s hope of a prize
Not quite. The article says: The believer’s lifelong effort, sustained by faith in the reward of the Hereafter.
questions.rationale: “As Helen Hoover laboured for over half a century… so the believer labours all his life for the attainment of reward in the Hereafter.”

questions.q: What does the article say is the harm in pampering children?
options: It costs parents too much money
Not quite. The article says: It makes them comfort-loving and unable to meet the demands of the world outside the home.
It makes children too fond of study
Not quite. The article says: It makes them comfort-loving and unable to meet the demands of the world outside the home.
It makes them comfort-loving and unable to meet the demands of the world outside the home
Well reasoned. Caring is good; pampering is not.
It causes quarrels between parents
Not quite. The article says: It makes them comfort-loving and unable to meet the demands of the world outside the home.
questions.rationale: “Pampering fosters an easy-going nature in children… They cannot meet the challenges which they have to face in the external world.”
